meta.tier_interpretation_note: These tiers reflect the probability (across years) that functional seasonal flow patterns are maintained to support native freshwater species (e.g., higher winter/spring mean daily flows than summer, and meeting functional-flow coverage thresholds). Legal standards rarely encode your exact functional-flow tier metrics; they influence outcomes by constraining reservoir operations, diversion/export limits, hydropower licensing conditions, water quality/water-right permit terms, and project-level mitigation. Likelihood scores reflect policy-to-outcome plausibility (strength/directness of operational leverage), not a guarantee of meeting any tier.

Legal Standards.name: Federal Endangered Species Act (ESA) — Section 7 consultation / Biological Opinions / RPAs (16 U.S.C. §1531 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Where listed aquatic species (or critical habitat) are affected, ESA can impose enforceable operational constraints on federal actions (including project operations) to avoid jeopardy/adverse modification—often translating into flow, temperature, ramping, and entrainment constraints that shape flow regimes.

key_elements.plain_definition: Process where a federal agency must evaluate and consult to ensure its action won’t jeopardize a listed species or damage its critical habitat.
The consulting agency’s determination about jeopardy/adverse modification, often including required conditions.
Required operational or project changes that allow the action to proceed without jeopardy.
Authorization/limits on unintended harm to listed species if certain measures are followed.

Legal Standards.name: California Endangered Species Act (CESA) (Fish & Game Code §2050 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: State analogue to ESA. For state/local projects and some operations, CESA can constrain activities that could ‘take’ listed species and can require avoidance/minimization/mitigation measures that affect instream flow, timing, and habitat conditions.

key_elements.plain_definition: Broadly, harming, killing, or otherwise adversely affecting a protected species.
A CDFW permit that can allow incidental take if impacts are minimized/avoided and fully mitigated.

Legal Standards.name: Clean Water Act (CWA) — Section 401 Water Quality Certification (33 U.S.C. §1251 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: For federally permitted/licensed projects that may discharge to waters, Section 401 allows the state to certify compliance with water quality standards and impose conditions (or deny), which can include flow/temperature-related requirements to protect aquatic uses.

key_elements.plain_definition: State approval (often with conditions) required before a federal permit/license can be issued if a project may discharge to waters.
Designated uses (like aquatic life) plus criteria/objectives intended to protect those uses.

Legal Standards.name: Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control Act (California Water Code §13000 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: California’s core water quality law. Water Boards adopt Basin Plans with beneficial uses and water quality objectives (which can include aquatic habitat protections). These objectives can drive operational requirements that intersect with flow and temperature regimes.

key_elements.plain_definition: The recognized uses of a waterbody (including ecosystem uses like fish habitat) that water quality rules must protect.
Numeric or narrative targets intended to protect beneficial uses (can include temperature/flow-related components).
Regional water quality control plan that lists beneficial uses, objectives, and implementation actions.

Legal Standards.name: SWRCB Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan (Bay-Delta Plan) (under CWA + Porter-Cologne; includes flow requirements and implementation tools such as D-1641 in the Delta context)
Legal Standards.note: A major statewide instrument establishing water quality control measures and flow requirements to protect beneficial uses (including fish and wildlife) in the Bay-Delta watershed—directly shaping operational flow/outflow requirements and sometimes seasonal patterns.

key_elements.plain_definition: The enforceable steps/requirements used to achieve water quality and flow objectives (often through operational rules and permits).
Operational obligations (e.g., minimum flows/outflow regimes) set to protect beneficial uses.

Legal Standards.name: California Fish & Game Code §5937 (dam flow requirement)
Legal Standards.note: Requires dam owners to pass sufficient water to keep fish downstream in ‘good condition’ (through a fishway or over/around the dam). This can translate into minimum releases and operational changes that affect seasonal instream flows below dams.

key_elements.plain_definition: A structure that helps fish move around a dam or barrier.
Enough flow to keep downstream fish populations in good condition (interpreted case-by-case).

Legal Standards.name: California water right permitting/public interest + Public Trust Doctrine considerations (SWRCB water-right administration; public trust balancing)
Legal Standards.note: SWRCB’s water-right decisions and ongoing administration can impose permit/license terms (e.g., bypass flows, instream requirements) and must consider public trust resources (like fisheries) when allocating water—often shaping flow protections and operational limits.

key_elements.plain_definition: A required amount of water that must remain in the river (not diverted) to protect instream uses.
Resources the state has a duty to protect for the public (commonly fisheries, wildlife, navigation, recreation).

Legal Standards.name: Water Code §1707 — Instream Flow Dedication (water right change to keep water instream)
Legal Standards.note: Allows rights holders to petition the State Water Board to change an existing right to dedicate water to instream beneficial use—creating a mechanism to legally protect flows in-stream (often targeted/local rather than basin-wide).

key_elements.plain_definition: A legal change to a water right so water stays in the stream for ecological/instream purposes.
The formal request process to modify a water right (e.g., purpose/place/use) to support instream flow.

Legal Standards.name: Federal Power Act (FPA) hydropower licensing (FERC licensing; fish passage and environmental conditions)
Legal Standards.note: Hydropower licenses can include mandatory fish passage prescriptions and fish-and-wildlife conditions and recommendations that affect dam operations—often including minimum flows, ramping rates, and seasonal regimes.

key_elements.plain_definition: Operational requirements attached to a hydropower license (often including flow and passage measures).
A required fishway/fish passage measure that must be included in a hydropower license where applicable.

Legal Standards.name: California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (Pub. Res. Code §21000 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Procedural law requiring agencies to analyze and disclose significant environmental impacts of discretionary projects and adopt feasible mitigation/alternatives where possible—often shaping project design and operations affecting instream flows, channel alteration, and habitat.

key_elements.plain_definition: The public agency with primary responsibility for approving/carrying out a project and ensuring CEQA review is done.
Feasible changes/conditions to reduce significant environmental impacts.

Legal Standards.name: Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta Reform Act of 2009 + Delta Plan consistency (Water Code §85000 et seq.; consistency requirements for covered actions)
Legal Standards.note: Governance framework requiring certain state/local actions in the Delta to be consistent with the Delta Plan, embedding ecosystem protection/restoration as a legally enforceable objective that can influence flow-related project decisions and constraints.

key_elements.plain_definition: A qualifying state/local project/action in the Delta that must certify consistency with the Delta Plan.
Written findings submitted to show a covered action aligns with Delta Plan policies.

Tier 1.threshold: Functional Ecosystem: Functional flows to sustain native freshwater species in 90% of years; Must have higher mean daily flows in spring and winter than summer.

policies.relationship: Strong alignment where flow objectives and implementation are stringent and enforced across key tributaries/operations
policies.note: Mechanism: Enforceable flow/outflow and water quality control measures can directly drive seasonal release/export constraints that help maintain winter/spring-dominant flow regimes in many years (system-dependent).

policies.relationship: Often strong for regulated systems when RPAs/BiOps impose seasonal flow and operational constraints
policies.note: Mechanism: ESA conditions can force seasonal flow, temperature, and diversion/pumping limits to protect listed species; achieving Tier 1 across 90% of years may require broader, sustained multi-tool implementation beyond ESA alone.

policies.relationship: Strong but geographically limited (dam-by-dam) lever for instream releases
policies.note: Mechanism: Minimum releases below dams can support functional flow components locally; Tier 1 at WBA/basin scale depends on coverage across multiple infrastructure points and hydrology.

policies.relationship: Strong in hydropower-regulated reaches; basin-scale outcomes depend on extent of hydropower control points
policies.note: Mechanism: License conditions can impose seasonal minimum flows and ramping requirements; Tier 1’s broad frequency requirement is harder where large non-hydropower diversions dominate the hydrograph.

Tier 2.threshold: Modified Functional Flows: Partial functional flows in wet season and spring; full functional flows in summer in 75% of years. Must have higher mean daily flows in spring and winter than summer.

policies.relationship: Direct lever likely to support partial functional-flow performance depending on objectives and compliance
policies.note: Mechanism: Flow requirements and implementation measures can shape wet-season/spring regimes and constrain diversions/exports, making Tier 2 plausibly achievable in more years than Tier 1.

policies.policy_name: Porter-Cologne + Basin Plans (flow/temperature objectives where applicable)
policies.relationship: Indirect-to-conditional lever (depends on how objectives are written/enforced and whether flow is the controllable pathway to meet objectives)
policies.note: Mechanism: If water quality objectives (e.g., temperature, habitat) require operational changes that effectively mean higher summer baseflows or spring pulses, implementation can support Tier 2 patterns.

policies.relationship: Conditional—strong for specific licensed/permitted projects (e.g., hydropower) rather than basin-wide
policies.note: Mechanism: 401 conditions attached to federal licenses/permits can require minimum flows, ramping, or temperature controls that improve seasonal flow functionality in affected reaches.

policies.relationship: Conditional—often meaningful for specific projects and operations affecting listed fish
policies.note: Mechanism: Avoidance/minimization/mitigation measures (including flow-related terms) can reduce harm and improve flow-related habitat conditions, helping move performance toward Tier 2 in some systems.

Tier 3.threshold: Existing Flow Requirements: CalSim minimum flow constraints for Baseline Scenario in 50% of years

policies.policy_name: SWRCB Bay-Delta Plan (existing implementation terms and minimum requirements)
policies.relationship: Direct—often maps to baseline minimum constraints captured in operations models
policies.note: Mechanism: Existing enforceable minimums (modeled as constraints) are a common reason baseline operations meet ‘minimum flow’ requirements in some fraction of years.

policies.policy_name: ESA (existing BiOps/RPAs reflected in operations constraints)
policies.relationship: Direct—often appears as operational constraints in baseline modeling assumptions
policies.note: Mechanism: ESA-driven operational constraints (e.g., minimum releases, export limits) are frequently incorporated into baseline operational rules, supporting Tier 3-type “existing minimums” outcomes.

policies.policy_name: Fish & Game Code §5937 (minimum releases below dams, where implemented)
policies.relationship: Direct but localized—often contributes to minimum-release constraints
policies.note: Mechanism: Where §5937 requirements have been operationalized, they can act like minimum instream release constraints that show up in baseline operations for affected facilities.

policies.policy_name: Water rights/public trust-based permit terms (bypass flows, instream conditions)
policies.relationship: Direct but variable—depends on permits and enforcement history in the basin
policies.note: Mechanism: Permit/license conditions requiring bypass flows or seasonal limits can create baseline minimum-flow constraints captured in operational modeling.

Tier 4.threshold: No function: none of the above thresholds met

policies.relationship: Weak-to-conditional as a driver (procedural) and may not overcome hydrology/senior demands/operational constraints
policies.note: Mechanism: CEQA can require mitigation/alternatives for specific projects, but it does not mandate achieving a functional flow regime; Tier 4 can persist even with CEQA if broader operations/demand dominate.

policies.relationship: Conditional—helpful where water is actually dedicated instream, but often not large enough or widespread to shift system performance alone
policies.note: Mechanism: Instream dedications can protect targeted flows; Tier 4 indicates dedications (if any) are insufficient in magnitude/coverage relative to hydrologic stress and competing demands.

policies.policy_name: Delta Reform Act / Delta Plan consistency
policies.relationship: Indirect governance lever—can shape decisions but not necessarily create enforceable functional flows by itself
policies.note: Mechanism: Consistency requirements can influence covered actions and align projects with ecosystem goals, but Tier 4 can persist without more direct flow-setting instruments.

Governing Agencies.name: State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB) + Regional Water Quality Control Boards
Governing Agencies.note: Adopt and implement water quality control plans (Basin Plans) under Porter-Cologne; administer CWA §401 certifications; develop and implement the Bay-Delta Plan (including flow requirements) and incorporate conditions into permits/orders that shape operational flows.

Governing Agencies.name: NOAA Fisheries (NMFS)
Governing Agencies.note: Leads ESA Section 7 consultation for many anadromous fish species and issues BiOps/RPAs that can impose operational flow/temperature constraints on federal actions; also participates in hydropower licensing contexts via fish passage/habitat expertise (as applicable).

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS)
Governing Agencies.note: ESA Section 7 consulting agency for species under its jurisdiction and a key fish-and-wildlife agency in hydropower licensing contexts, including fish passage prescriptions and recommendations that can affect flow regimes.

Governing Agencies.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
Governing Agencies.note: Issues and enforces hydropower licenses under the Federal Power Act; incorporates mandatory fish passage prescriptions and other environmental conditions that often include minimum flows, ramping, and seasonal operational measures.

Governing Agencies.name: California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW)
Governing Agencies.note: Implements CESA (including Incidental Take Permits) and provides biological expertise and conditions/mitigation recommendations (often affecting instream flow, timing, and habitat) in CEQA and permitting processes.

Governing Agencies.name: Delta Stewardship Council (DSC)
Governing Agencies.note: Implements the Delta Reform Act’s Delta Plan and oversees the Delta Plan consistency program for covered actions, which can constrain or reshape projects affecting flow-related conditions in the Delta.
